↳ Posted by emily_bmore on April 13th, 2004.

Hop Jigs are just a way of playing a slip jig. A hop jig is played faster with a feel almost like a waltz, the first note of each triplet gets the emphasis. If lilted it would get a sort of Dowdle deedle dum feel. Slip jigs are played way slower with more of a dowd-el-y deed-le-y dum.

↳ Posted by b.maloney on April 13th, 2004.

Michael Gorman

This tune was made popular as the title track of a Kevin Burke/Micheal O Domhnaill Green Linnet LP. Kevin picked up the tune from a ten-inch Folkways disc recorded in London in the 1950s by the piper Willie Clancy and fiddler Michael Gorman. The liner notes described it as the music for the “promenade” or first figure of a set dance once common in south Sligo, and even provided a description and diagram of the dance. There was no real title on the disc, but Kevin called it “Promenade” for this reason. It has been published as “Coleman’s,” but was never recorded by Michael Coleman, only by Gorman.

↳ Posted by Fernando Durbán Galnares on October 31st, 2020.

As played by Micheal Gorman - the original tune IMO

This (X:6) is my “bare bones” transcription of a recording titled Michael Coleman’s Hop-Jig by Michael Gorman (track #2 on the album The Sligo Champion). Here’s a link for that:
https://open.spotify.com/track/01YMnj0UVyK5gMTL9Tv9wc
(The youtube link given by Steve Owen in a comment 8 years ago, above, is no longer working.)

A friend lent me this album, and from the sleeve notes this particular recording was made by Sean Davies in London, 7 July 1964. The given source for the tune is: “Michael Coleman before he left Sligo”.

---

Listening to the recording, it seems to me that Gorman’s playing a completely different tune from the one played by Kevin Burke. Of course, it’s extremely closely related. His tune is in a fast, swung, nervous 3/4. I see it as the “old-time” way of playing slip jigs.
It reminds me of the Silver Slipper as played by Tommy Peoples or John Doherty.

It’s clearly related to the Kevin Burke tune, that’s given in the other (9/8) settings here. But for me it’s really not the same tune. For want of better descriptors, let’s call the 9/8 tune the slip-jig tune, and let’s call Gorman’s tune the hop-jig tune.

What’s fascinating to me is the relationship between the two. It seems to me that the slip-jig tune is derived somehow from the hop-jig one by shifting the “one” beat and making a few other tweaks. It’s a great example of how tunes change, evolve and transform into something quite new.

I believe the hop-jig to be the older, original tune.

---

I also made a more detailed, involved, transcription of the recording, to try to get closer to all the good stuff in M Gorman’s playing. I’ll post that next.

---

Re: Coleman’s

I’ve listened a ton to Michael Gorman, actually - that’s one of the original places I learned the tune, and I’ve played it for well over a decade and a half, at least.

I’m not sure how you’re hearing the pickup notes as a downbeat, but the strong push on that E with the bow is much stronger than on the pickup notes. Note as well that on the Irish Pipes and Fiddle tunes LP he’s playing different pickup notes all together. It’s also clear in the B part that the phrasing doesn’t follow how you wrote it.

Personally, even with the strong swing pulse, I’d still always write hop jigs in 9/8, but I do understand the reasoning behind the choice for 3/4. The actual swing is in between, of course.

Re: Coleman’s

GoPlayer, I completely agree with Nico here. At the start of the tune, Gorman plays the pick up notes very deliberately and at a slower tempo, basically as crotchets (quarter notes), which is a common enough way to start a tune in this tradition. But they’re still just pick up notes.

The correct downbeat note is the open E string.

Your transcript renders the tune in a way that no trad musician would play it.

Re: Coleman’s

I didn’t actually post any links. There are indeed three distinct recordings of it from Gorman, and it’s clear from listening to all three that you’re mishearing the tune and pulse. Especially since in all three he doesn’t play the same initial pickup notes (which also don’t appear again on repeats).

I don’t really think there’s anything particularly unique about the way he plays these types of tunes, or this specific tune. Everyone I hear playing it plays it with more or less then same pulse and phrasing, including Kevin - speaking of Kevin, he may have learned it from Gorman or Jimmy Power, the latter of whom would be very good for you to listen to, too, as I’m sure he got the tune direct from playing with Gorman.

I’d recommend listening more until you can hear it correctly! Good luck!
